content: RHOT1, also known as Mitochondrial Rho GTPase 1 (MIRO1), is an enzyme encoded by the RHOT1 gene located on chromosome 17 in humans. This protein is a member of the Miro protein family and plays a critical role in mitochondrial transport by anchoring mitochondria to the motor/adaptor complex. Through its involvement in mitochondrial transport, RHOT1 contributes to mitochondrial homeostasis, apoptosis, and has been implicated in diseases such as Parkinson’s disease (PD) and cancer. Structure In mammals, RHOT1 is one of two Miro isoforms, the other being RHOT2 (Miro2). Both isoforms share a structural organization that includes two EF-hand motifs linking two GTP-binding domains and a C-terminal transmembrane domain. The transmembrane domain anchors the protein to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM). The EF-hand motifs serve as binding sites for the adaptor protein Milton and the kinesin heavy chain. These motifs can also bind calcium ions, and calcium binding induces a conformational change that detaches mitochondria from kinesin. Function RHOT1 belongs to the Rho GTPase family and is one of the two Miro isoforms, RHOT1 (Miro1) and RHOT2 (Miro2). Unlike other members of the Rho GTPase family, Miro isoforms are atypical due to their unique regulatory mechanisms and exclusive expression in mitochondria. Miro proteins interact with Milton (TRAK1/2) and motor proteins such as kinesin and dynein to form the mitochondrial motor/adaptor complex. This complex tethers mitochondria to the cytoskeletal microtubules, enabling their transport within cells. While Miro has been extensively studied in neurons, it also facilitates mitochondrial transport in lymphocytes toward inflamed endothelial regions. The activity of the motor/adaptor complex is regulated by calcium ion levels. At high calcium concentrations, calcium ions bind to Miro, causing the complex to detach from mitochondria and arrest mitochondrial transport. This regulatory mechanism is thought to localize mitochondria to areas of high calcium ion concentration, such as dendrites and axons, where they buffer calcium ions and maintain cellular homeostasis. Miro also regulates mitochondrial fusion and mitophagy in conjunction with mitofusin proteins. In one proposed model, damaged mitochondria are segregated from healthy ones through the degradation of Miro and mitofusin. Miro degradation halts mitochondrial movement, while mitofusin degradation prevents fusion with healthy mitochondria, facilitating their clearance by autophagosomes. Additionally, RHOT1 has been implicated in promoting caspase-dependent apoptosis, although the precise mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated. Clinical Significance Research suggests that Miro proteins may play a role in Parkinson’s disease (PD). In neurons, Miro interacts with two key proteins associated with PD, PINK1 and Parkin. Following mitochondrial depolarization, PINK1 phosphorylates Miro at multiple sites, including S156, and Parkin ubiquitinates Miro, targeting it for proteasomal degradation. The degradation of Miro halts mitochondrial transport, a process critical for maintaining mitochondrial quality control. Although the Rho GTPase family is closely associated with cancer progression, there is limited evidence linking the atypical Miro proteins to cancer. However, RHOT1 has been implicated in pancreatic cancer as a tumor suppressor through its regulation of mitochondrial homeostasis and apoptosis. This suggests that RHOT1 could serve as a potential therapeutic target for cancer treatment. Model Organisms Model organisms have been employed to study the function of RHOT1. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Rhot1tm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi, was developed as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This initiative aims to generate and distribute animal models of human diseases to researchers. In these studies, male and female mice underwent standardized phenotypic screening to assess the effects of RHOT1 deletion. Notably, no homozygous mutant mice survived until weaning, indicating the essential role of RHOT1. Heterozygous mutant adult mice exhibited no further abnormalities in the remaining tests. Interactions RHOT1 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including: ALEX3, DISC1, Dynein, HUMMR, Kinesin heavy chain (KHC), Mitofusin (MFN1/MFN2), Milton (TRAK1/TRAK2), Parkin, PINK1, and OGT.
